title: Tiling window managers
description: Tiling managers lay out windows with no overlap and no manual dragging: the screen is recursively split (binary space partition), each window takes a tile, and keyboard commands rearrange. i3, Sway, and tmux panes all work this way. The algorithm is a tree — split a leaf vertically or horizontally — and every layout operation is a tree rotation away.
mechanism: BSP tree: leaves are panes, internal nodes are splits (direction + ratio). New pane splits the focused leaf. Operations: split, close (merge), rotate, resize (adjust ratios).
algo: O(depth) per operation; layouts are trees, not pixel math.

title: Tab groups
description: Tab groups organize documents beyond one row of tabs: VS Code's editor groups (split right, split down), browser tab groups (colored, collapsible). Each group is an independent tab strip with its own active tab; drag moves tabs between groups. The data model is groups -> tabs -> documents; the UI renders the tree.
mechanism: Group = {tabs: [...], active: tab}. Operations: move tab across groups, split group, merge. Persist group layout per workspace.
algo: O(1) tab ops; layout persist is a tree serialization.

title: Diff panes
description: Diff panes show two versions side by side with changes aligned: the diff algorithm (Myers) computes the edit script, and the panes scroll together with change hunks highlighted and aligned. Three-way merge panes add the base. The hard part is alignment — keeping both panes' lines matched as you scroll — which the edit script provides directly.
mechanism: Myers diff -> hunks; render both sides with aligned rows (padding for inserts); synchronized scroll; hunk navigation (n/p). Merge: 3 panes + result.
demo:
import difflib

a = ['line1', 'line2', 'line3', 'line4']
b = ['line1', 'line2 CHANGED', 'line3', 'line4', 'line5']

sm = difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, a, b)
left, right = [], []
for tag, i1, i2, j1, j2 in sm.get_opcodes():
    la, lb = a[i1:i2], b[j1:j2]
    n = max(len(la), len(lb))
    la += [''] * (n - len(la)); lb += [''] * (n - len(lb))
    for x, y in zip(la, lb):
        mark = ' ' if x == y and tag == 'equal' else '*'
        left.append('%-14s %s' % (x, mark)); right.append('%-14s %s' % (y, mark))

print('%-18s | %s' % ('LEFT', 'RIGHT'))
for l, r in zip(left, right):
    print('%-18s | %s' % (l, r))

title: Synchronized scrolling
description: Synchronized scrolling keeps panes aligned: scroll one, the other follows. For diffs, alignment is by matched lines (not pixels) — the scroll maps through the alignment table. For independent documents, it is proportional (same fraction). The implementation is a scroll listener translating offsets through the mapping; smooth-scroll animation must not fight the user's hand.
mechanism: Alignment map: line_a <-> line_b. On scroll: new_offset_b = map(offset_a). Proportional fallback: fraction * height. Debounce; disable during user drag on the target.
algo: O(1) per scroll event via the map.
demo:
# scroll maps through the alignment table (diff panes), not pixels
# alignment: left line -> right line (None = gap)
align = {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: None, 3: 2, 4: 3}  # left line 2 deleted on right

def scroll_right(left_line):
    r = align.get(left_line)
    if r is None:  # gap: interpolate between neighbors
        below = min(k for k in align if k > left_line and align[k] is not None)
        r = align[below]
    return r

for l in range(5):
    print('left line %d -> right line %s' % (l, scroll_right(l)))
print('independent docs: proportional (fraction x height) instead')

title: Drag-drop layout
description: Drag-drop layout lets users build their pane arrangement by dragging: drop zones highlight (left/right/top/bottom/center of a pane), and the drop splits or tabs accordingly. The implementation is hit-testing the pointer against zone rects during the drag, with a ghost preview of the resulting split. Touch needs larger zones and a long-press to start.
mechanism: Dragstart: capture the pane. Dragover: hit-test 5 zones per pane under the pointer; show ghost. Drop: apply split/tab operation. Esc cancels.
algo: O(panes) hit-test per move event; trivial.

title: Layout persistence
description: Layouts persist across restarts: serialize the split tree (directions, ratios, tab order, active tabs, scroll positions) to the workspace state, and restore it on open. The format must be versioned — old layouts load into new versions gracefully. Dirty editors restore too (backed by the backup system), so the window reopens exactly as left.
mechanism: Serialize BSP tree + per-pane state to JSON; version field; migration functions per version. Restore lazily (visible panes first). Autosave on change (debounced).
demo:
import json

layout = {'v': 2, 'root': {'split': 'vertical', 'ratio': 0.6,
          'a': {'tabs': ['main.py'], 'active': 'main.py', 'scroll': 120},
          'b': {'tabs': ['test.py'], 'active': 'test.py', 'scroll': 0}}}

def migrate(d):  # v1 -> v2 added 'scroll'
    if d['v'] == 1:
        d['v'] = 2
    return d

saved = json.dumps(layout)
restored = migrate(json.loads(saved))
print('restored v%d:' % restored['v'], restored['root']['a'])
print('versioned format + migrations: old layouts always load')

title: Focus management
description: Focus management decides where keystrokes go: the focused pane gets input, focus follows the mouse optionally, and keyboard commands move focus directionally (focus left/right/up/down). Focus must be visible (highlight the active pane) and predictable — stealing focus is a bug, not a feature. Modal dialogs suspend pane focus and restore it on close.
mechanism: Single focused-pane pointer; focus events on click/shortcut; directional focus = spatial search among pane rects. Focus-visible styling. Dialogs push/pop focus.
algo: O(panes) directional search; O(1) focus set.

title: Multi-cursor across panes
description: Multi-cursor editing spans panes: cursors in different files edit simultaneously, each pane rendering its own carets. The implementation keeps a cursor list per pane with a shared command bus — type once, apply everywhere. Selections can differ per pane. It shines for parallel edits (rename across files, aligned data).
mechanism: Cursor set per pane; edit commands broadcast; each pane applies to its cursors independently. Undo is per-pane (or grouped). Carets rendered per pane.
algo: O(cursors) per keystroke; trivially parallel per pane.

title: Preview panes
description: Preview panes show a read-only rendering beside the source: Markdown preview, image viewer, PDF, webview. They update on save (or on type, debounced) and scroll-sync with the source. The security model matters for webviews — sandboxed iframes with a strict CSP, no node access. Preview is a second pane type, not a mode.
mechanism: Source pane -> render pipeline (debounced) -> preview pane. Scroll sync via anchor mapping. Webviews sandboxed (CSP, no remote code).
algo: O(doc) render, debounced; sync O(1) via anchors.

\1

', html, flags=re.M) def on_type(new_src): global last_render, rendered, src src = new_src now = time.time() if now - last_render > 0.3: # debounce 300ms rendered = render(src) last_render = now return 'rendered' return 'debounced' print(on_type(src + '!')) print(rendered.replace('\n', ' | ')) print('webviews: sandboxed iframe, strict CSP')

title: Split limits and performance
description: Every pane costs: an editor instance, syntax highlighting, language server features. Beyond ~6-8 panes the costs compound — memory, CPU, and the user's attention. Editors mitigate with pane virtualization (only visible panes fully active), shared language servers, and honest limits (warn, don't crash). The performance budget per pane is what sets the practical split limit.
mechanism: Virtualize inactive panes (keep state, drop heavy resources); share language servers across panes; lazy-restore on focus. Monitor per-pane memory; warn past the budget.
algo: O(visible) heavy resources; state kept for all.

title: Keyboard control of layouts
description: Layouts must be fully keyboard-driven: split, close, move focus, resize, move panes between groups, toggle maximization — all without the mouse. The command set is small (~15 commands) and must be discoverable (command palette lists them). Resize uses discrete steps with repeat; maximization is a toggle, not a layout change.
mechanism: Command registry for layout ops; directional focus; ratio adjust by steps; maximize = overlay flag (layout preserved underneath). All in the palette.
algo: O(1) commands on the BSP tree.

title: Session restore
description: Session restore reopens everything: panes, tabs, unsaved buffers (from the backup store), scroll positions, even terminal histories. The backup system writes dirty buffers continuously, so a crash loses seconds, not work. Restore is staged — window frame first, then panes lazily — so the app feels instant even with 50 tabs.
mechanism: Continuous backup of dirty buffers; session snapshot (layout + open files + states); staged restore (frame -> visible panes -> rest). Crash recovery uses the same path as normal restore.
algo: O(open files) backup; staged restore feels O(1).
demo:
import json, time

# hot exit: dirty buffers backed up continuously; session snapshot on quit
backups = {'main.py': ('print(1)', time.time())}  # content + timestamp
session = {'layout': 'split-v(0.6)', 'open': ['main.py', 'test.py'], 'active': 'main.py'}

saved = json.dumps({'backups': backups, 'session': session})
# ... restart ...
r = json.loads(saved)
print('restored layout:', r['session']['layout'])
print('restored tabs:', r['session']['open'], '| dirty buffer main.py intact:',
      r['backups']['main.py'][0] == 'print(1)')
print('crash loses seconds (backup cadence), not work')

title: Plugin panes
description: Plugin panes let extensions add their own pane types: terminals, notebooks, custom editors, webviews. The host provides a pane API (create, dispose, serialize state, toolbar contributions); the plugin renders inside. Sandboxing keeps a crashing plugin from taking the layout down. The API surface is small but must be stable — plugins outlive host versions.
mechanism: Pane contribution point: view type + factory + serializer. Host manages lifecycle; plugin renders content. Webview-based for untrusted code; native for trusted.
demo:
# host pane API: plugins register a view type + factory + serializer
registry = {}

def register_pane(view_type, factory, serialize):
    registry[view_type] = (factory, serialize)

register_pane('terminal', lambda: 'pty-instance', lambda p: {'cwd': '/tmp'})
register_pane('notebook', lambda: 'notebook-ui', lambda p: {'cells': 3})

print('registered:', list(registry))
# host lifecycle: create -> serialize on quit -> restore
factory, serialize = registry['terminal']
pane = factory()
print('created:', pane, '| serialized:', serialize(pane))
print('crash in one plugin pane must not take the layout down')

title: Pane performance profiling
description: Pane performance is profiled per pane: which pane's highlighting, extensions, or preview pipeline burns CPU. The tooling attributes costs to panes (editor render time, extension host time per pane) so users can find the slow one. Budgets: 16ms frame, <100ms tab switch, <1s restore. Profile before optimizing — the slow pane is rarely the one you guess.
mechanism: Per-pane timing (render, extensions, preview); flame attribution; budgets enforced in CI on synthetic layouts. Startup profiling for restore.
algo: O(panes) attribution; budgets as CI gates.
demo:
import time

# per-pane cost attribution (synthetic)
costs = {}
for pane, work in [('editor', 12000), ('terminal', 800), ('preview', 45000)]:
    t = time.perf_counter()
    sum(i*i for i in range(work))  # simulated render work
    costs[pane] = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000

for pane, ms in sorted(costs.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    flag = ' <- OVER 16ms budget' if ms > 16 else ''
    print('%-9s %7.2fms%s' % (pane, ms, flag))
print('attribute per pane; the slow one is rarely the one you guess')

title: Testing layouts
description: Layouts are tested, not eyeballed: unit tests for the BSP operations (split/close/resize invariants), serialization round-trips (save -> load -> identical), fuzzing random operation sequences (the tree must stay valid), and screenshot tests for the common arrangements. Fuzzing finds the bugs — random splits and closes violate invariants humans never try.
mechanism: Invariant checks (ratios sum, leaves = panes); round-trip tests; operation fuzzing with invariant asserts; visual regression on canonical layouts.
demo:
import random
random.seed(1)

# fuzz BSP ops; assert invariants after every op
leaves, splits = [{'id': 0}], []

def check():
    assert len(leaves) == len(splits) + 1, 'leaves = splits + 1 violated'

for step in range(200):
    if random.random() < 0.7 or not splits:
        leaf = random.choice(leaves)  # split a random leaf
        leaves.remove(leaf)
        leaves += [{'id': leaf['id'] * 2 + 1}, {'id': leaf['id'] * 2 + 2}]
        splits.append(leaf['id'])
    else:
        splits.pop()  # close a split (merge)
        leaves.pop()
    check()
print('200 random split/close ops: invariants held (leaves = splits + 1)')
print('fuzzing finds the bugs humans never try')
